opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think a lot further than people expect, but probably not all the way, at least not soon.

The thing that slows enterprise adoption down today isn't really the model. It's everything around the model. You walk into a big bank or a telco, and their data is scattered across dozens of systems: some of it is in a modern cloud warehouse, some is in a SharePoint nobody's touched since 2014, some is in a mainframe. There are permissioning rules, compliance constraints, and a lot of tribal knowledge about which system is the source of truth for what. Historically, getting a model plugged into all of that has been a services-heavy exercise. You send in forward-deployed engineers, they spend weeks mapping it out, building connectors, writing evals, tuning retrieval.

A lot of that work is very automatable. Writing a connector against a documented API, figuring out a schema, generating test cases, even drafting the eval suite for a workflow. Agents are already pretty good at those things, and they're getting better quickly. So I think the setup time drops dramatically, from months to weeks and eventually maybe days for a lot of standard deployments.

Where I think humans stay in the loop for a while is in two places. First, judgment about what to automate and what "good" looks like. An agent can build you an eval, but somebody inside the business has to say "this is the outcome we care about, and this is the failure we can't tolerate." That's a business decision, not a technical one. Second, trust and security. Enterprises are rightly cautious about letting an autonomous system wire itself into their core infrastructure and grant itself access. So you'll see agents doing the heavy lifting, with humans approving the sensitive steps: access grants, anything touching customer data, anything that writes back into production systems.

So my honest view is that the integration layer becomes mostly agent-driven, the governance layer stays human for a good while, and the companies that win will be the ones that make that handoff between the two feel really seamless.

r001.rationale: The response predicts substantial automation of enterprise integration work while saying it will not be fully automated soon, with humans retaining judgment, governance, and approval of sensitive steps.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think we're a lot further along than people realize, and I also think the ceiling is further away than people realize. Let me take both halves of that.

On the "further along" side: most of what enterprise integration actually consists of is not deep intellectual work. It's reading documentation, understanding what fields exist in a Salesforce instance or a ServiceNow schema, figuring out how to authenticate against an API, writing glue code, and then testing that the glue code does what you think it does. That is squarely in the sweet spot of what these models are good at today. A model that can read your API spec, look at your data, and write and run the connectors is already a real thing. So the part of the integration bill that used to go to a systems integrator sitting in a conference room for six months, a lot of that is going to collapse. I think that's not controversial anymore.

Where it gets harder is that the hard part of enterprise deployment was never the code. The hard part is the organization. Who owns this data? Which of the three versions of "customer" in your systems is the true one? What is this agent allowed to do, and who is accountable when it does something wrong? Those are governance and trust questions, and an agent can't resolve them for you, because they're not technical problems. They're decisions. What the agent can do is surface them much faster. It can tell you, "Look, you have conflicting definitions here, which one do you want?" And that compresses the timeline, but it doesn't remove the human from the loop on the decisions that matter.

The other thing I'd flag is that enterprises are rightly skeptical of anything that touches production systems autonomously. We've spent years with customers building confidence incrementally. First the agent reads and proposes. Then it writes with approval. Then it writes in a sandbox. Then, eventually, it acts. I don't think you can skip those stages, and I don't think you should. So my prediction is that the setup and integration work becomes almost entirely agent-driven, but with a human sign-off layer that persists for a long time, maybe permanently for the high-stakes systems. The economics change dramatically. The accountability structure changes slowly. And I think that's the right way for it to go.

r001.rationale: The response says agents will handle nearly all setup and integration work while humans retain governance decisions and sign-off, especially for high-stakes systems. This communicates that automation will not cover the entire process.

astra-6.text:
I think quite far. A lot of enterprise AI setup is connecting systems, figuring out where the relevant data lives, and translating a business process into something the model can actually work with. Those are tasks that agents can help with, and increasingly take on themselves.

The harder part is knowing what success means. If you’re automating a workflow, somebody has to decide what the system is allowed to do, which mistakes are acceptable, and when it needs to ask a human. An agent can help you work through those questions, but there’s still a business decision underneath them.

So I’d expect the integration work to become much less manual. You describe the outcome you want, the agent examines the systems it has access to, proposes an implementation, and helps test it. Then you expand its autonomy as you get evidence that it works. That could make deploying AI accessible to a much broader set of businesses.

r001.rationale: The response expects agents to take on much of the integration work, while leaving success criteria and acceptable autonomy as business decisions. This communicates likely partial automation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think quite far. A lot of the work in getting AI deployed inside an enterprise is connecting it to the right data, giving it access to tools, and figuring out how to evaluate whether it’s doing the job well. Those are all things that agents can help with, and increasingly carry out themselves.

But there’s a difference between getting a demo working and having something you trust in production. You have to understand permissions, handle exceptions, and know when the system should ask a human for help. And often the hardest question is: What do you actually want this process to do? That requires people in the business to make decisions.

So I expect a lot of the technical setup to become automated. The human work shifts toward specifying the outcome, setting boundaries, and checking that the system is delivering what you intended.

r001.rationale: The response expects agents to automate much of the technical setup, while people still specify outcomes, set boundaries, and check results—so it predicts partial rather than complete automation.
